Note: I tend to be an intuitive cook, almost every single ingredient will be "to taste."

Ingredients

  • 1lbs shrimp
  • 1lbs fettuccine
  • garlic cloves
  • olive oil
  • butter
  • garlic powder
  • paprika
  • salt
  • red pepper flakes
  • dry white wine (I use Sauvignon Blanc)

When you're selecting your shrimp, remember that the shell adds flavor. I usually do peeled and deveined with tail on. Better than no tail, but a lot less work than having to remove the shrimp from the sauce and remove shells.

  • Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil.
  • Finely chop your garlic. I use about 6 cloves.
  • Add olive oil to a large skillet on medium-high heat. Use a good olive oil; nothing is worse than shitty oil.
  • Sautee garlic and red pepper flakes until garlic starts to color. I use a lot of red pepper flakes. I literally have no idea how much, but it's at least 2 tablespoons. Maybe more.
  • Once garlic is fragrant and beginning to color, add butter to skillet, about half a stick. This cools the garlic so it won't continue to cook and burn.
  • Add shrimp, cook until done. I season lightly with paprika.
  • Add fettuccine to the boiling, salted water. Use good fettuccine. Trust me, bottom shelf pasta is disgusting. Pay the extra 40 cents and get the nice stuff.
  • While fettuccine cooks, add white wine to skillet. I use about 1/3 of a 750 mL bottle each time I make it. Turn heat to high and cook until wine is reduced. You'll know it's ready when it looks like the wine is gone.
  • When pasta is cooked, drain and return to the pot. Add sauce and coat pasta.

Serves 4.

That looks solid. As for being an "intuitive cook", I translate that to "experienced cook". Once you get a feel for how shit works together you don't need exact measurements, and tend to just eyeball it. With exception of baked goods, I haven't followed a recipe exactly in probably a decade, because I've worked in kitchens and know how food works.
Spices also tend to lose flavor over time, and fresh is obviously more potent than dried. So it's important to just have a good sense of what you are doing.

Yep. It helps to keep your spices as whole, untoasted, and unground as possible until you're ready to use 'em. Unground spices kept in a lightless airtight container will last a pretty long time in most cases. Whole nutmeg can last years with little reduction in flavour. Whole black pepper too.

My favorite cooking tip that was given to me is to put a little ground sea salt down on a cutting board when you chop garlic. The salt absorbs some of the juices and keeps it from becoming a wet, sticky mess.
